Chicken mince patties, on a "rice cake", with warm fennel and cauliflower salad, and sweet potato puree (x-posted from v/food)

Chicken Patties: 500gms chicken mince 3 basil leaves finely chopped half a tsp of tumeric 1 egg shredded cheddar cheese (approx 1/4 cup) shredded parmesan cheese (approx 1/4 cup) 1 can diced tomatoes a handful of spinace leaves - roughly chopped paremsan cheese for the top

pre-heat oven to approx 150 celcius.

place mince, and all other ingredients, minus the tinned tomato and spinach, into a bowl, and mix together. heat a skillet with some oil (i used coconut), and spoon some chicken into the pan and flatten to desired thickness. sear it on each side, remove and place on a plate to cool for a bit.

in a baking dish, pour the tinned tomatoes in, and spread evenly across the bottom. evenly place the chicken patties into the baking dish, sprinkling the spinach and extra parmesan over the top. optional: add a few perino, or cherry, tomatoes, chopped in half. place the dish in the oven and cook for about 40 mins, or until the top looks nice and golden.

whilst the chicken is cooking, boil up some rice - approx. 1 cup. you'll need to make sure it's a little sticky so that it keeps it's shape should you choose to shape it. i used one of the kids sandwich boxes as the mould. once the rice is cooked, just spoon it in and flatten it until it looks like it's going to stay put.

with the sweet potato: i simply steamed a few slices of peeled and diced spud until it was soft. using a fork, and butter, i added and "smooshed" until it was smooth enough for my liking. optional: a pinch of powdered ginger to spice up the flavour of the potato.

the fennel and cauliflower was just chopped to desired volume, and steamed until tender.

i had a few baby truss tomatoes floating about the fridge, so i just placed them in the skillet on a low heat, and covered until the skin split a little.

B-HOP on Feinting

Boxing is a very demanding sport mentally and physically, every move you make, make sure there is a reason behind it.

 

Possible uses of feinting:

  • Feint to see your opponents’ reaction (identify patterns) and later create opportunities behind it. Example

  • Feint to restart your opponents. Buying time to think and space. Make sure you’ve establish certain respect beforehand, otherwise he won’t probably react to the feint. This point goes hand to hand with the first point. :D

  • Feint; exploit your opponents’ guard before attacking. Example

  • Feint to control distance, not just to make him back up but also to get closer. Make your foe pay attention to your hands, arms or eyes but steadily (with small steps as you feint) close the distance and when you are ready take offensive. You can also lean on your back foot to give the illusion that you are even further away, slowly creep closer with your lead foot then explode. Example

  • Feint to cause reaction and counter it. Example

 

These are just some uses, there are always endless possibilities. In order to be creative in the ring you have to do this stuff beforehand (heavy bag, shadowboxing, pads, imagining it, etc.), so when the time comes you’ll have the confidence knowing that mentally and physically you can perform what you want.

"Don’t feint just to feint"

The thing about the US is its fucking huge and as varied as the whole of the EU is.

The land itself is insanely varied. On the east coast you have warm temperate climate with massive deciduous forests. There is a 2,200 mile (3,500 km) long hiking trail that follows a mountain range up the eastern side of the country..

Further to the east on the other side of the Appalachians you get rolling hills of Ohio, Kentucky, and the Cumberland Plateu of Tennessee which is awesome as its kind of like a giant wall of land. Florida is hot and south of the panhandle the ground is mostly sand with the water table normally a few feet below the ground.

The middle of the country is flat and fertile. States like Nebraska, Iowa, Kansas, are the Great Plains and the bread basket for the nation. Miles and miles and miles and miles of corn fields. Their flatness results in massive storms as cold air from Canada collides with hot wet air from the Gulf of Mexico. The storm fronts can spawn massive tornadoes that obliterate everything beneath them. To the south you have Louisiana which is somewhat similar to Mississippi and Alabama in its geography until you get near the coast which is VERY swampy. The deltas of Louisiana has a demographic that only exists there, the Cajuns.

As you get closer to the Rocky Mountains the geography changes. To the north you have Montana and Wyoming. Big Sky country. The ground here is so flat and sparse of trees that it can feel like you will almost fall off the planet into the sky. Standing in the plains of Wyoming you might be the tallest thing for miles. Yellowstone is to the western side between the two states, I can't fit Yellowstone into a single sentence, go read the wiki, incredible place.

South of that the land becomes arid and desert. Colorado, Utah, Nevada, Arizona, New Mexico all have incredible geography with foothills of the rockys and desert canyons. Bryce Canyon, the Grand Canyon, Monument Valley all capture the incredibly beauty of it. There is also many desert basins in this area.

After that you hit the West Coast. California is more arid to the south and fertile to the north. Above Cali is Oregon which is lush and wet. Above that is Washington State, Oregon and Washington are very wet as cool air flows down from Canada squeezes moisture out of the warmer Californian air, the Rockies help hold the moisture in place so both states are known to be very wet. The colossal redwood forests are in Oregon and northern California. All three west costs states are very hilly and mountainous.

Hawaii and Alaska are both unique and incredible. Hawaii is a volcanic island paradise, each island has its own personality and I could write pages on each. Alaska is massive, larger than Texas, very mountainous, very cold. Massive boreal forests and taiga cover most of the state. Insanely wild and beautiful.

America is massive and various states can be worlds different. The people even more so.

Traditionally, Japanese is written in a format called tategaki (縦書き?), which is inspired by the traditional Chinese system. In this format, the characters are written in columns going from top to bottom, with columns ordered from right to left. After reaching the bottom of each column, the reader continues at the top of the column to the left of the current one.

Modern Japanese also uses another writing format, called yokogaki (横書き?). This writing format is horizontal and reads from left to right, as in English.

A book printed in tategaki opens from what someone native to Latin-based writing systems would call the back, while a book printed in yokogaki opens from what traditionally in Japan would have been considered the back.
